name: Fly.io
summary: Fly.io turns your Docker image into fast-booting Firecracker microVMs on its own servers in regions around the world, and routes each user to the nearest one.
intro: Fly.io runs apps on Fly Machines: Firecracker microVMs on physical servers that Fly.io owns, in 17 regions. `fly launch` scans your source code, can generate a Dockerfile for frameworks such as Phoenix, Laravel, Rails and Django, and writes a `fly.toml` config; `fly deploy` builds the image and rolls it out; `fly scale count 3 --region iad,fra,sin` spreads Machines across cities. Under Fly Launch sits the Machines API, a REST API for creating, starting, stopping and destroying individual VMs, which you can also call directly.

Every app gets shared IPv4 and IPv6 addresses announced over BGP Anycast from all of Fly.io’s data centers, so a user’s connection lands at the nearest one. A Rust proxy on every server terminates TLS and forwards the connection to the closest running Machine, over WireGuard if it is in another region. The proxy can also stop or suspend idle Machines and start them again when requests arrive; a stopped Machine boots in well under a second, and while stopped you pay only for its root filesystem.

A Machine’s root filesystem is ephemeral. For data that must survive, a Fly Volume is a slice of an NVMe drive on the same physical server, attached to one Machine and not replicated. Billing is per second for running Machines: the smallest, a shared-cpu-1x with 256 MB, costs $2.19 per 30 days. New organizations get a short trial but no free tier.
strengths: One app can run in many regions with one command, and Anycast sends each user to the nearest Machine
Any Docker image runs inside its own Firecracker microVM, a stronger boundary than containers sharing a kernel
Autostop and autostart cut the bill for quiet apps: a stopped Machine costs $0.15 per GB of root filesystem a month and restarts in under a second
The Machines API gives direct control of individual VMs, so you can build your own functions platform or per-user environments on it
limits: Volumes live on one server in one region with no replication; if the drive fails that Machine goes down, so Fly.io tells you to run at least two and replicate data yourself
The ephemeral root filesystem is capped at 2,000 IOPS and 8 MiB/s whatever the Machine size

Autostop never creates Machines: the most that can run is the number you created, its stop loop runs every few minutes and stops at most one Machine per region per pass, and `min_machines_running` only applies in the primary region
No free tier for new organizations: the trial lasts 2 hours of Machine runtime or 7 days, then a credit card is required

story: Kurt Mackey had helped build Ars Technica and spent much of that time making the site fast. A content delivery network made pages fast for anonymous readers, but paying subscribers wanted personalized pages and community features that the CDN couldn’t speed up, so they waited on servers far away (often in Virginia). The fix, Mackey argued, was to run the app itself close to users rather than bolt a CDN onto an app in one region.

Fly.io launched in 2017 and went through Y Combinator in Winter 2020. In the Launch HN post that March, Kurt, Jerome and Michael described it as “a platform to run Docker applications close to end users”: Fly.io converted a Docker image into a root filesystem, booted it in Firecracker VMs, and used a Rust router, Anycast IPs and a WireGuard mesh to send each user to the nearest VM, with three commands to deploy to 17 cities. The founders had grown up on Heroku and modeled deploys on it. For its first year the platform was that proxy plus a HashiCorp Nomad driver that started Firecracker.

In May 2022 Fly.io opened Fly Machines, VMs controlled by a REST API that boot in about 300 ms, built so apps could scale to zero. In 2023 it began moving apps from Nomad to flyd, its own orchestrator (internally “AppsV2”), because Nomad expected federated regional clusters and asynchronous placement, while Fly.io ran one global cluster of many small apps. In October 2024 it discontinued its plans with free allowances; new organizations now pay as they go.

choices.why: Fly.io runs many customers on the same hardware, and Thomas Ptacek wrote that Docker’s isolation “isn’t strong enough for that”, so it unpacks each container image into a Firecracker microVM instead.

choices.choice: Its own hardware, not another cloud
choices.why: TechCrunch reported that most investors first thought running its own physical servers was silly, but came around once they saw it was cheaper than EC2 instances and let Fly.io control its costs.

choices.choice: Run the app near users instead of a CDN
choices.why: Mackey called a CDN “a misfeature for most developers building dynamic applications”, because the app still runs in one region; Anycast plus a global proxy moves the whole app instead.

choices.choice: Create Machines ahead of time, start them on demand
choices.why: Pulling a large image to a distant region can take minutes, so Fly.io made Machines cheap to keep stopped. Starting an existing Machine skips the slow part and makes scale to zero practical.
